review_text:
I find this game to be very beautiful in terms of art style. It is sometimes really difficult to see the parts to eh item that you're looking for, but you get used to it eventually. Or that's what the hint button is for.

The story itself uses old fairy tales that are re-imagined. I personally like it and the entire series of Dark Parables are all interlinked.

Recommended if you like HOP style games and are looking for something new.

Dark Parables #1. A series of fragmented object games with puzzles and stories that each stand alone, but are also interconnected in the form of recurring characters. But each game tells its own story and they can technically be played in any order.

This being the first game, it is quite old and devoid of any bells and whistles like fast travel, collectibles, or achievements. It does come with a bonus adventure, however. 

Also, be warned, some of the fragmented object scenes are quite difficult because the pieces are very well disguised -- you really need sharp eyes for this one.

This is a tentative yes from me.

This is VERY MUCH the first game in a series, and it shows. The art in the game is beautiful, for sure. The game plays smoothly without crashing and the story, while rudimentary, makes sense (which is somehow not guaranteed in this genre.) If you can get it on sale, it's a worthy play.

And now, for the complaining.

My primary problem is that the hidden object scenes were all of the same type, where the single key item you need from the scene has been broken into pieces and the only things you look for in the scene are the shattered pieces of the one item. The scenes themselves are generally pretty simple and unobjectionable, but there's very little sense of triumph when finding all the pieces without help - or any sense of regret when having to use a hint to find the last vaguely-triangular wood-textured chunk hidden on a pile of firewood. I abused the living daylights out of the Hint button in the second half of the game.

The puzzles were few and still somehow repetitive. The final puzzle also stretched on for far too long as a "boss fight."

I mentioned the story was rudimentary, and it is. I found that any potentially interesting twists in the tale were all expository, either in the opening cutscene or in the ending cutscene, tossed in as an "oh, by the way,  XYZ thing could have happened if you had failed, but you didn't! :)" The bonus chapter also had a couple throwaway details that could have made for an upending revelation but just kind of sat there as window-dressing instead.

I will be getting the later titles in the Dark Parables series, because I do see potential for the storytelling to improve, but it's definitely kind of a rough opening act.

Beautiful little old gem. I've played this game years ago on BFG and couldn't resist purchasing it and playing it again on steam. This game is a fragments scene heavy, it's not the usual hidden objects game you play. The narrative voice over was good, but the main character doesn't speak at all. The journal wasn't 100% helpful, and the fact that there is no map or even fast traveling (except at later in the game and only in one spot) cause too much backtracking.
 
Dark Parables series are all connected to each other, the characters will be mentioned in the games this is why I highly recommended you to play them in chronological order of their release.

Keep in mind this game is old, this is why I recommend it to people who like this casual point & click game and doesn't expect something like the newest HOGs.

Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose is a solid hidden object game with an interesting twist on the classic tale of Sleeping Beauty. This game also holds the promise of a continue of a longer story arc through each Dark Parable game, so they may have to be played in order if you want to  follow that.

Story aside, the gameplay is a little different from most hidden object games. There are plenty of hidden object scenes to go around (at least three per chapter, I think!), however instead of finding a random list of objects in the scene, you find pieces that will combine to make an object needed in order to progress. It makes for interesting finding, although it can become a little repeatitive and sometimes pieces can be a little too well hidden. 

As for the other key gameplay mechanic of hidden object games, i.e. puzzles, Curse of Briar Rose has some interesting ones. The puzzles were fairly diverse, and different from many of the one's I had personally seen before. Some even had multiple stages, or phases to go through before completion. All in all, I never really wanted to skip the puzzles, which is always a plus.

Now, what about graphics and music? Graphics-wise, the game is pretty. The scenes very pretty, and generally fit the fairytale feel of the game. As for the music, it was also quite nice, setting the tone and mood easily.

What's also nice is the game comes with a little bonus content. A strategy guide you can access while in the game, an extra chapter to play, and things such as wallpapers and extra puzzles to unlock at the very end. 

The only negetive things I can think to say is that the lack of a map made it a little hard to navigate sometimes, and that again, some objects were just a little too hidden.

Overall, Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose is a great game, easily earning an 8/10 from me, and I recommend you give it a try.

Originally released in 2010 and developed by Blue Tea Games (based in Hong Kong) and published by Big Fish. Dark Parables: The Curse of Briar Rose is a reinterpretation of the Sleeping Beauty story but with a few slightly darker themes to it than is usually expected. Reset in Scotland, you are sent as an investigator to uncover the mystery of the abandoned castle. It’s a fairly basic premise but it does set up the basics of a plot that is further developed through the subsequent games.

[list][h1]Pros[/h1]
[*]Lavishly portrayed scenes
[*]Collectable objects that reduce your time penalty when using hints
[*]Lots of additional features such as an inbuilt walkthrough and wallpapers

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[*]Quite a bit of backtracking
[*]Very short
[/list]
Upon arrival at the castle, your first problem is to gain access to the grounds, and then later on the various buildings themselves. The game is incredibly light on your motivations and providing you with any compelling reason to be there, other than that you are. It is vaguely frustrating and in terms of character motivation, the game is incredibly weak. It does make up for this though with the beautiful grounds and intriguing puzzles that are presented.

The gameplay itself is what has become standard for Hidden Object Games now, yet even though some aspects are now outdated, the game still holds incredibly well, nearly 10 years after its initial release. It is a Fragmented Object game, that will have you searching for various pieces that should fit together to create an object you require. There are also light adventure game elements with these and other tools you encounter on your journeys. It isn’t terribly innovative in these elements either but they are satisfyingly executed. The only possible issue was the amount of backtracking, which became frustrating quite quickly. No areas are locked though and the whole grounds become available to you as you progress in the story… and at a late stage of the game, a shortcut is unlocked to assist you with moving about. 

Many of the quests you are given are usually to obtain an item to gain access for the next area, or triggering a new event to advance the story. (Hence the need for backtracking) but it’s altogether a generally pleasant experience without too much frustration. Obtuse puzzles do not prevail here, and if one does become vaguely confused there is a hint button that highlights important areas while adventuring or missing objects during the Hidden Object scenes. The short puzzles you face may also be skipped but they are fairly generic and should be familiar to most veterans of the genre. The hints are timed at intervals but gathering collectable morphing items (hidden on nearly every scene) will reduce this time penalty.
In addition, the Collector’s edition actually comes with a full guide and walkthrough built into the game, so even if playing on the expert mode, which grants you no hints, there should be no frustration with finishing this title. It is a little on the short side, as I finished it in a mere two hours, however, there is also the bonus adventure that foreshadows events in the sequel.

The UI and interface are comfortable to use, with small detailed embellishments that suit the theme of the game but truly the game does shine with its rich baroque environments, and lush detailed scenery. Small animations accompany some scenes to give them some life. The graphics themselves have been adapted to fit HD and widescreen which is extremely useful considering how much visuals have advanced over the years.

As a creative retelling of the Sleeping Beauty tale, The Curse of Briar Rose is an intriguing premise. As the first in the series, it is somewhat bareboned when compared to its sequels, which sadly doesn’t give it much potential for replays. And due to its short duration, it doesn’t offer much value for money either. It is however well worth picking up as part of a Dark Parables bundle or as a single title on discount.

[b][u]Game Information[/u][/b]

"Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose" Collector's Edition is a Fragmented Object game. The game was developed by Blue Tea Games and published by Big Fish Games Studio.

"Curse of Briar Rose" is the first episode of "Dark Parables."

Since this is a collector's edition game, it comes with extra features that are not available in its counterpart; the standard edition.

[b][u]The Game Review[/u][/b]

Game Visuals

I want to mention that the visuals for the game are nicely done. The visuals can be adjusted in the game's option menu.

Game Audio

I want to mention that audio for the game is well done. Even though the audio is somewhat simplistic and repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu as well.

Gameplay

There are no game difficulty modes to choose from. When the game is being played for the first time; it is in normal mode. When the game is being played for the second time; it is on hard mode.

The notebook keeps track of the progression in the game. Such as story events and clues.

There is no map available in the game. The player has to remember where to go in the game.

There is no padlock feature that is available to lock the inventory panel in place to make it stationary. The inventory panel automatically comes stationary.

The hidden object scenes consist of the following: Fragmented items. Some of these hidden object scenes may require a little or no interaction.

The puzzles in the game are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them.

There are morphing objects (beyond objects) in the game. They are scattered throughout the game for the player. The morphing objects are used to refill the hint bar.

Since this is a collector's edition game, there's a bonus chapter, but it can be accessed only after the main story is completed.

Miscellaneous

There are extra features in the game: Bonus Chapter; Wallpapers; Screensavers; Music; Concept Art; 3 Novels and Game's Strategy Guide. Most of these extra features can be accessed only after the entire game is completed.

Final thoughts: I have found the game enjoyable to a certain extent. The replay value for the game is low. I would recommend this game, but not at the game's full price value.

[b]Dark Parables 1: Curse of Briar Rose[/b] (FROG) 
([i]January, 2012 review updated in April, 2019 after playing Steam version[/i])

ENORMOUS spider alert!

The Steam interface does not work with this game, but I had no trouble getting it to go full-screen.

Options are separate sliders for Music and Sound, and Full-screen or Windowed.  There IS an expert mode (no hints or skips available), but it does not unlock until you play through the game once.

The Dark Parables games are [b]FR[/b]agmented [b]O[/b]bject [b]G[/b]ames (FROG's). For those not familiar with the genre, instead of finding items by list or silhouette, you need to find pieces of items, which will them form an in item that will go into your inventory. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1703472539

Dark Parables puts their own spin on the story of Sleeping Beauty, and it makes for an interesting game that holds up to this day.

EVERYTHING you see and every inventory item you collect is pertinent to the story. There are no misplaced or out-of-time items that I saw.  
 
I will say right up front that I generally do not enjoy this sub-genre as much as standard HOG's, but the Dark Parables games are an exception. [i]Curse of the Briar Rose's[/i] fragmented object scenes are so masterfully-integrated into the artwork that they are challenging, but never frustrating to find.  Some of the pieces  you're supposed to be finding will be different colors than what is pictured in your to-find list, but this is realistic.  Items [i]do[/i] take on the reflected colors of the scenery around them, and the artists took this into account beautifully. 

You will examine some of the HO scenes up to three times, but it will look different each time you visit, and every time is just as interesting as the first.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1703473706

HINTS are refillable during the HOS.  An interesting touch with the hints is that if you pick up an inventory item, then hit the hint button, it will show you where the item can be used.

Being one of the very early FROG's made - and the first game in this series - there is no map, no insta-transport, and indeed, no hints for the adventuring portion of the game... At least not what today's gamer would expect.  Instead of using a HINT, there is an Inspect button, which will bring up small pictures of the locations that you need to investigate.  Since there is a LOT of to-ing and fro-ing in the game, this is super-helpful!  Once you've done all of the FROG scenes for a chapter, the Inspect option will instead offer to give you an Objective Hint. Using this feature will give you a three minute penalty on your hints, and will show you a small picture representing what you need to do.

As mentioned above, there is a lot of back and forth in  his game, but they added a shortcut later in the game that will greatly-reduce how much ground you need to cover - a nice touch!  

Puzzles can be skipped, but there is a five minute hint penalty.  The puzzles themselves range from inventive (early on) to a marble puzzle that repeats a few times.
 
The combination of the music and the dark-but-beautiful graphics makes the game very immersive, despite being HO-heavy.
 
When you finish the main game, you will obtain a golden rose, that will 1. Allow you to play the game on Expert Mode, and 2. Give you access to a room that you couldn't get into on your first play-through.

[b]CE Content:[/b]
[list]
[*]20 Cursed (morphing) items, which will instantly refill your hint meter
[*]Integrated Strategy Guide
[*]Bonus Chapter
[*]5 Wallpapers
[*]Screensaver
[*]7 Music tracks
[*]Novels (three different interpretations of the story of Briar Rose)
[*]Concept Art (three versions of five different scenes)
[*]20 Bonus (marble) puzzles
[/list]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1703477422

The Bonus Chapter is about 30 minutes long, and needs to be completed in order to unlock the bonus content (except for the morphing items and strategy guide).  There is a repeating memory game that is EXTREMELY difficult during this bonus chapter.  I actually skipped them after the first time, as they were just too much for me.

I thoroughly enjoyed revisiting Curse of Briar Rose after all of these years, despite not being a fan of Fragmented Object Games.  The game is lovely and immersive, and I found that I really enjoyed all of the to-ing and fro-ing, just so that I could enjoy take in the environment.  Definitely recommended!

I bought this Game just recently in the Steam Winter Sales as I have been waiting for ages for this Game to go on Sale and I must say I dont regret it.

Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose Collector's Edition comes with the Main Story which is around 3 and a half hours long and a Bonus Chapter which gives you another half to an hour. It also comes with Extras, such as Wallpapers, Music, Mini Games and Concept Art. For the first time in a Point & Click / HO Game I actually saw that there was a bit a backstory to read within the Game. 

This is the First dark Parables Game in the Parables Series and I must say although the resolution was unchangeable and there was no Steam Overlay, I did really enjoy it.

It reminded me a bit of [url=http://steamcommunity.com/id/BabyVampireBat/recommended/32140?snr=1_5_9__402]Midnight Mysteries[/url] just with a far less Grimm Art Style. The Voice Acting was surprisingly good compared to other HO / Point & Click Games and the atmosphere was gorgeous! 

It seems that this game just like Midnight Mysteries actually do depend on playing them inline unlike Grimm Legends where you can just play them backwards Numbered if you so wanted to.

Similiar to Midnight Mysteries this Game also comes with a Strategy Guide that helps you via Pictures and writing to find your way if you lost it or help you on Puzzles if you get stuck on them. Which is to me personally a huge plus so I dont need to alt+tab out and search for half an hour on the web.

The Hidden Objects were very well hidden and sometimes difficult to spot especially to its low native resolution. However once you get used to it, you should be able to find your way around just fine.

All in all this Game is a great & Atmospheric Point & Click / HO Game that I can recommend to anybody that loves a good story or those Kind of Games. However due to the fact that this Game is rather short with hardly any Options in the Settings Menu I recommend getting it on Sale as its base price seems a bit to high.

This is one of my very favorite hidden object series and Briar Rose is the first game! What I like most about the series is that the games are FROGs (fractured (or fragmented) object game) as opposed to HOGs (just hidden object games). Every piece found in a hidden object scene is used to create one item that goes into inventory.

Pros:
o beautiful graphics
o fractured hidden object scenes (ingenious!)
o interesting take on the Sleeping Beauty fairy tale
o strategy guide included

Cons:
o extremely slow hint & skip recharges (although not needed so not a problem)
o no interactive map (although the INSPECT does help find hidden object scenes)
o Simon Says mini-games in the bonus chapter (I skipped them all... I think there were only two)
o no Steam cards or achievements (something fixed in the following games in the series)

I purchased and played the first 5 games in the series elsewhere but plan on playing them all again on Steam!

This is the first game of the long-running series Dark Parables, and as such many features that would be taken for granted in later versions are absent here, but it doesn’t make it any less interesting. The whole series has this ongoing lore following the Fairytale Detective’s adventures, and many characters and references would show up in later episodes.  
It is pretty much what says in the tin: the curse of the Briar Rose seems to be spreading, and the player needs to investigate the castle and reach the princess’ chamber to wake her up and break the curse altogether, being guided by the princess and facing the opposition of the Evil Godmother watching your every move.
I think the hidden objects segments are a little harder than the following games to the point of some objects being very close to the background there are placed against. The pacing isn’t so obvious at times, with some backtracking not being signaled at all: it is assumed you will go back to every previous hidden object location once a new chapter begins to see if they have something new. Flaws aside, it is a pretty solid title and it would take a little over three hours to beat, a promising start that comes with a teaser and seeds for an overarching mystery.  The graphics are outstanding with well-crafted backgrounds that while rich in detail won’t overload with too much information and the soundtrack has a haunting and ethereal quality that upholds the mystery and the feeling of being at an enchanted castle.

Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose successfully interprets the classic story of Sleeping Beauty but puts its spin on things in order to provide a fresh look at its narrative. There’s nothing terribly wrong with this HOPA but in terms of story, you feel more could have been done with the source material. The concept of these classic stories existing in reality to be investigated is intriguing but the story plays out in a fairly pedestrian manner which may send a few players to sleep themselves.

Dark Parables is one of these series with many games in it, in the world of casual gaming. Curse of the Briar Rose is one of the four (or five?) developed by Blue Tea Games, before the series was given to another studios. I've played one of the recent entries and I can see the improvements.

Curse of Briar Rose is the tale of Sleeping Beauty, though you're a Fairy Tale detective, going from fairy tales places to another. In this case, you're sent to a town where Briar Rose/Sleeping Beauty is rumored to be sleeping since a thousand years, despite the prince managing to lift a part of the curse. Right now, vines are invading and it's a sign that the curse is stronger and that the Evil Godmother is ready to come back.

I liked the plot, it's not really the problem in this game. It's interesting to be a detective exploring either the tales or the aftermath.

My main problem is the gameplay. I'm so used to the modern one that I felt that Briar Rose was totally a step back... and it has a reason: Curse of Briar Rose was released years ago. Here, you find items in different locations but the majority of them are in hidden objects scenes. That's my problem here: it's only find parts of objects, with a picture of them. Those are often hard to spot, either because they're too small or they're blending with the background. After a while, it was really boring. It's just frustrating. As for the puzzles, while they're only a few, they're often the same. Another problem for me is the lack of map to fasten the travel. Also, while the "Inspect" feature is nice to help you to find where to go, by moments, I found myself stuck because I didn't know where to go. In other words, it wasn't always clear where to go for using a specific item. Indeed, the Inspect feature is only there to show where hidden objects scenes are available. In other words, if you didn't pay attention entirerly to locations, you're just lost.

The graphics are decent though I was under the impression to have a grainy screen, which made me take some distance with the atmosphere of the game. The soundtrack is nice.

Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose is really showing its age and the gameplay isn't the most interesting and isn't even well balanced. While the plot is good, I found myself bored and stuck. I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone wanting to discover the genre, it's just for the hardcore players. And even for them, it might not satisfy them.

Well, as much as I like most hidden object games, I can't really say I enjoyed this one.

It is obviously rather dated, in presentation, content, plot and game mechanics. No doubt it was decent back when, but I just found it a chore.

I have two main objections:
- The 'hidden object' scenes are all the 'find random pieces of something you aren't at all familiar with by using the pictures' kind. I've never really liked these, and they are relentless here. This is compounded by dull backgrounds for the most part, so you are looking for small brown or grey things on a brown or grey background. And the orientation, size and colour of objects in the scene often don't even match the picture clues. Even when I used a hint on some items, it was quite hard to make out what I should be clicking on. 
It is also compunded by my second main issue:

- The game refuses to work even vaguely in full screen mode on a mode HD monitor. Even changing the resolution and trying to run in windowed mode ended up with some of the game (mostly the item bar at the bottom) being cut off, even though there was plenty of screen space left. So I was running in a tiny window. Frankly it was a headache; it certainly gave me one. I know this was possibly developed before HD was generally available, but it's been on Steam for less than two years, and if a developer is going to re-release on Steam I'd think it was the least they could do to revisit it and make sure it works adequately with current hardware.

Other points to note are that there is no map (not necessarily bad). The hints are mostly useless, just telling to go to this location or solve this problem next. Presented in completely unreadable, tiny thumbnails which again was compounded by the resolution problem. The Strategy Guide was more helpful on the occasions I got bored of wandering randomly about hoping to find something new.

Plot? Well, I suppose you could just about find one. Detective goes to castle to rescue people from spreading thorn infestation. Wakes up princess who's under an evil spell. That's it. And it really isn't elaborated on in any way at all. The bonus game is even lacking in that level of context.

As I said; I really like HOGs, but although it was possibly okay when released, I really can't recommend it today with so many much better examples of the genre available.

[h1]Short version: 30%[/h1]
Only play Dark Parables 1 if you are interested in the entire series. Otherwise, get ready for constant eyesore and endless backtracking.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Even a long fragmented object series like Dark Parables has to start somewhere. The problem is that it starts with the Curse of Briar Rose.

I mean, yes, I get it. FROGs must have non-descript item fragments. It is the definition of the genre. However, when the scenes are almost pitch black, and the pieces are barely a few pixels in size, then the game stops being fun and starts to torture the players.
Curse of Briar Rose is not only full of such scenes but loves to repeat them several times. It also likes to forget to tell the player if they have to return somewhere. Maybe because you have to backtrack anyway.

There are some puzzles next to the terrible fragment scenes and backtracking, and they are fantastic. While they cannot save the score much, at least they show some promise for the rest of the series.

As for the story, there isn't one to speak of. We are a fairy tale detective, and we must search every pebble of Briar Rose's old castle. This is it.

The only reason I'm not recommending this game is some of the objects are nearly impossible to see. I need to use the hint button too often. Also, I said "no" to the tutorial but still get prompts that won't go away unless I do what they say even if I don't want to perform that action right away. Very annoying. No tutorial means leave me alone. Not going to play again. Uninstalling.

This is [I]Dark Parables[/I] #1, a lackluster retelling of the Sleeping Beauty classic.

Hidden-object games are only as good as their hidden-object scenes. In this case, they are awful. They are actually hidden-fragment scenes, where the challenge is to recognize a handful of pixels against the similarly-colored, low-resolution backdrop. There's nothing satisfying about solving these.

I'll say one good thing about the game: the drawings are lovely and many. But the gameplay is so bad that it's impossible to recommend.
